extracted.intended_audience: U.S. literate public and policymakers in 1862 (Congress, border-state citizens, Maryland officials)
extracted.subtask_description: Policy‑proposal essay arguing a specific program of gradual emancipation, colonization, compensation, and financing for border and rebel states during the U.S. Civil War, using census and actuarial calculations to justify costs and benefits. Focuses especially on Maryland and similar border states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer pecuniary aid to states for gradual abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Congress offered pecuniary aid to such States as would gradually abolish slavery within their limits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal government should financially assist loyal states that adopt a program of gradual emancipation; the offer is presented as a central inducement to peaceful abolition rather than coercive immediate emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonization of manumitted slaves by the Government (with consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The colonization, from time to time, of the manumitted slaves, with their consent, by the Government, beyond our boundaries, was also contemplated as a part of the system."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonization (emigration assistance to settle freed persons abroad) is a component of the proposed plan and must be voluntary—requiring the consent of the manumitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: General emancipation in rebel states as a military necessity (compensation only to loyal masters)
rubrics_metrics.description: "As to the States persisting in rebellion after the close of this year, the President, as a military necessity, has announced a different measure, that is, general emancipation in all such States, with compensation only to loyal masters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where rebellion continues, emancipation may be compulsory as a war measure; compensation is limited to owners in loyalty to the Union, not to rebel masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject immediate universal emancipation with full compensation as impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Immediate emancipation of all slaves, with compensation for all, costing, as it would, twelve hundred millions of dollars, is now beyond the power of the Government... Nor was such a measure ever wise or expedient."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues against an immediate, universal compensated emancipation on fiscal and policy grounds, advocating slower, staged approaches instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the Pennsylvania/Benjamin Franklin model: free the 'post nati' (children born after the law)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great model act of gradual emancipation, drawn by Benjamin Franklin... adopted by Pennsylvania in 1780, liberated all the descendants of slaves born after that date within the limits of the State... I shall call those born before the date of emancipating laws the ante nati, and those born after the date of such laws, post nati."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggested legal model is to immediately free children born after the law (post nati) while leaving existing adults (ante nati) to be phased out over time—presented as humane, practicable, and fiscally modest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship of emancipated post nati until age twenty-one under same regulations as white apprentices
rubrics_metrics.description: "...the emancipated post nati would remain apprentices until they reached twenty-one years of age, under the same regulations, mainly, as were applicable to white children, bound out by the overseers of the poor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of gradual emancipation, newly freed children should remain bound as apprentices until 21 to facilitate transition and labor arrangements, using existing poor‑law apprenticeship mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation standard example: use sworn expert valuations (e.g., $50 per infant)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the execution of the emancipation act of Congress in this District, infant slaves were valued officially this year by sworn experts at $50 each."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official sworn expert valuations as the basis for compensation calculations; the essay applies the $50 per infant figure to census infant counts to estimate first‑year costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund emancipation by issuing United States stock (government bonds) bearing fixed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sum of fifteen millions of dollars of United States stock, issued now, and bearing interest at the rate of six per cent, per annum, would make all the border States free States..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes financing emancipation through government debt instruments (six percent U.S. stock), i.e., issuing bonds now to cover manumission costs and spread fiscal burden over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use census data and life‑expectancy tables to compute costs and declining annual liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: "By the census... the post nati numbered... which, at $50 each, would cost... This sum... would decrease every year. According then to the annual tables, and those of expectancies of life (as calculated for me)..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological prescription: rely on census counts (by age) together with actuarial life‑expectancy tables to estimate the immediate and declining future cost of freeing post nati and to size financing appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set an explicit target date for complete emancipation if states consent (example: July 4, 1876)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Should the border States consent to proceed more rapidly, I have no doubt the Government would cheerfully pay to loyal masters such additional sum as would give freedom to every slave in all the border States, on the 4th of July, 1876..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a concrete time horizon as a political negotiating device—the centennial date is proposed as a symbolic and achievable deadline for full emancipation in border states if they choose an accelerated plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make emancipation a war measure to withdraw slaves from support of rebel armies
rubrics_metrics.description: "...it is our duty, after the close of this year, to withdraw the slaves in the rebel States from the culture of the crops used to support their armies, which can only be done by general emancipation in such States persisting then in the rebellion. This is a necessary war measure..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames emancipation not only as moral/political policy but as a legitimate military strategy aimed at undermining the enemy's logistical/economic base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate loyal citizens for slaves manumitted by the government
rubrics_metrics.description: "...full compensation is contemplated by Congress and the President, in all cases of the manumission by us of the slaves of loyal citizens."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that compensation funds should be paid to loyal owners when the federal government manumits slaves (distinguished from rebel owners), as part of an equitable settlement to gain border‑state cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic justification: show emancipation increases wealth, population, and revenue beyond costs
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is a smaller sum than four months' cost of the war, whilst wholly and forever removing the discordant element... The augmented wealth... would soon return to the Government, in increased revenue, a sum far exceeding the cost of gradual emancipation and colonization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require cost‑benefit analysis demonstrating that the long‑term gains (increased population, productivity, revenues) outweigh immediate expenditures; treat emancipation as an investment in national prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative metrics (population density, mortality, shore line, natural resources) to evaluate slavery's impact on state progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "We must consider the area, soil, climate, mines, hydraulic power, location, shore line, bays, sounds, and rivers... The census proves that our progress as a nation has been greatly retarded by slavery... The population... per square mile... mortality... shore lines..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prescribes specific comparative indicators—population per square mile, mortality rates, shore line miles, presence of coal/iron and hydraulic power—to empirically support claims that slavery retards demographic and economic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gradual, legislative, and inducement‑based change over sudden coercive measures (except as military necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If this measure seems slow in securing total manumission and colonization, it would be progressive and certain... Would we avoid like disasters in solving this stupendous problem, we must follow... gentle, but constant and successive movements..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative imperative: favor gradual legislative programs and persuasion/inducement to remove slavery to avoid social upheaval—except where rebellion justifies sudden military emancipation.
